overview: Kanem was the eastern Lake Chad heartland of a long-lived state. Its rulers joined Saharan networks, while archaeological work reveals substantial brick-built elite settlements. Its beginnings remain uncertain.

items.text: Elite builders used fired bricks for residences and enclosures. Tié is a candidate for the capital Njimi, not a securely identified location.
The Arabic Diwan preserves a dynastic chronicle. It helps historians reconstruct royal succession, while requiring comparison with other evidence.
Trade across the Sahara exchanged enslaved people for horses, cloth and manufactured goods. Cultural exchange coexisted with coercion.
Sayfawa rulers adopted Sunni Maliki Islam. Royal religious change should not be treated as a single conversion date for every community.

sources.title: Carlos Magnavita, Susanne Lindauer and Adoum Casimir Adjbane, New Luminescence and Radiocarbon Dates for Kanem-Borno Fired-Brick Elite Sites (2025)
Rémi Dewière, The Kanem and Borno Sultanates (11th-19th Centuries) (2024)
